title: Maximum flow: Edmonds-Karp vs Dinic
problem_statement: Given a directed network on vertices 0..n-1 with non-negative integer edge capacities (parallel and antiparallel edges allowed), a source s and a sink t != s, compute the value of a maximum s-t flow.

input.parameter: n = V = number of vertices; E denotes the number of edges.
input.size_measure: V + E edges with capacities (at most 100 in the harness), so arithmetic on capacities and flows is unit cost. Both bounds below are strongly polynomial (independent of the capacity values).

algorithms.name: Edmonds-Karp
algorithms.idea: Ford-Fulkerson with shortest augmenting paths: repeatedly find a fewest-edge s-t path in the residual graph by BFS and push its bottleneck capacity.
algorithms.pseudocode: while BFS finds an s-t path P in the residual graph: push min residual capacity along P
algorithms.time_complexity: O(V E^2): O(V E) augmentations of O(V + E) each (Edmonds & Karp 1972); O(V^5) on dense graphs
algorithms.correctness: Ford & Fulkerson 1956: a flow is maximum iff the residual graph has no s-t path (max-flow min-cut theorem); with integer capacities every augmentation adds at least 1, and Edmonds & Karp 1972 bound the number of shortest-path augmentations by O(V E) independently of the capacities.

algorithms.name: Dinic (blocking flows)
algorithms.idea: Phases: build the BFS level graph of the residual network, then saturate it with a blocking flow found by depth-first searches with current-arc pointers. The s-t distance grows every phase.
algorithms.pseudocode: while t is reachable: levels = BFS(s); push a blocking flow along level-increasing edges (DFS with current-arc pointers)
algorithms.time_complexity: O(V^2 E): at most V - 1 phases, O(V E) per blocking flow; O(V^4) on dense graphs
algorithms.correctness: Dinic 1970. Augmenting only along level-increasing edges keeps every augmenting path shortest. After a blocking flow every s-t path in the new residual graph is strictly longer, so there are at most V - 1 phases. Termination when t is unreachable gives a maximum flow by the max-flow min-cut theorem.

relationship: Upper bounds O(V E^2) -> O(V^2 E) (O(V^5) -> O(V^4) on dense graphs), both cited (Edmonds & Karp 1972; Dinic 1970); the second upper bound is smaller whenever E = omega(V). No lower bound for Edmonds-Karp is shown here, so this entry does not show that Dinic is asymptotically faster. Edmonds-Karp spends a full BFS on each augmenting path. Dinic finds all augmenting paths of the current shortest length in one O(V E) blocking-flow phase. Both are worst-case upper bounds; the measured growth on random networks is far below both (see verification).

sources.authors: Ford, L. R.; Fulkerson, D. R.
sources.title: Maximal flow through a network
Theoretical efficiency of the Edmonds-Karp algorithm for computing maximal flows
sources.note: Studies the theoretical efficiency of the Edmonds-Karp algorithm (per its title); the paper was not read for this entry, and nothing from it is used or implemented.

verification.method: V1: both implementations agree with each other and with an independent oracle on random digraphs (densities 0.15, 0.4, 1.0; capacities from [1, 100], [1, 3] or unit; with zero-capacity, parallel and antiparallel edges), layered networks and networks with t unreachable, n = 2..10, 12, 14 (oracle: minimum over all s-t cuts, by enumeration) and n = 30, 60 (oracle: only the bounds 0 <= flow <= min(capacity out of s, capacity into t)). Not raised to V2 (INCONCLUSIVE): no instance family attaining either worst-case bound was constructed. On the random dense networks of generate_scaling (G(n, 0.5), n = 20..160), experiments/2026-10-07_max_flow_probe.py measured alpha = 0.558 for Edmonds-Karp against V E^2 = Theta(n^5) and alpha = 0.479 for Dinic against V^2 E = Theta(n^4); both would fail. The counts explain why. Edmonds-Karp made 21, 40, 87, 176 augmentations for n = 20, 40, 80, 160 (about n, far below V E = 3820 ... 2040640), and Dinic needed only 4, 3, 2, 3 phases. Against lower powers the same timings gave alpha = 0.924 vs n^3 for Edmonds-Karp and 0.965 vs n^2 for Dinic. That is average-case growth on this family, not a test of the claimed bounds, so it is not recorded as a V2 claim.

caveats: Both time bounds are worst-case bounds that random networks do not approach; this entry does not demonstrate them empirically (V1). With integer capacities both implementations run in O((F + 1)(V + E)) time, where F is the maximum flow value: every augmentation raises the flow by at least 1, so there are at most F augmentations; every breadth-first search reads each adjacency list at most once; and every Dinic phase except the last augments at least once, so there are at most F + 1 phases, each costing O(V + E) plus O(V) per augmenting path. Since F <= C outdeg(s) for maximum capacity C (the cut around s), capacities <= 100 without parallel edges out of s give F <= 100 (V - 1) and O(V (V + E)) time. So in that range, which includes generate_scaling, Dinic's O(V^2 E) is not attained along any sequence of networks with V -> infinity, and Edmonds-Karp's O(V E^2) along none with E -> infinity; on generate_scaling both run in O(n^3). Zadeh 1972 studies the efficiency of Edmonds-Karp (per its title; the paper was not read here); no worst-case construction is claimed or implemented in this entry. Faster algorithms are catalogued in staging/max-flow-edmonds-karp-vs-almost-linear. On the random networks measured here Dinic was also faster in practice (6.0 ms vs 39 ms at n = 160 in one console run), but that is not evidence for the worst-case bounds.
notes: Maximum bipartite matching is the unit-capacity special case (compare pairs/bipartite-matching-kuhn-vs-hopcroft-karp). The two algorithms here differ only in how much is done per BFS: one augmenting path (Edmonds-Karp) or a blocking flow (Dinic).
